title: Zechariah 12:1–9
context: A new oracle concerning Israel begins with the LORD, who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the human spirit. He will make Jerusalem a cup of reeling and a burdensome stone for the surrounding peoples. When the nations gather against the city, the LORD will strike their horses with terror and blindness, strengthen the chieftains of Judah, save the tents of Judah first, and defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the feeble become like David and David’s house like God, like the LORD’s angel. Readers in both traditions hold several options for these oracles: events in Israel’s later history, a symbolic picture of God preserving his people and the church, or a future deliverance of Jerusalem. These notes present them as options, with no winner between the traditions. The Judges 9:23 box treats how the traditions describe the LORD’s rule over hostile nations.

verses.text: A revelation of the LORD’s word concerning Israel: The LORD, who stretches out the heavens and lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him says:
verses.arminianNotes: A revelation of the LORD’s word concerning Israel: Arminian readers see the LORD introduced as Creator of the heavens, the earth, and the human spirit, grounding what follows in his power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD forms the spirit of man within him. The creation language assures hearers that the one who speaks can do what he promises.

verses.text: “Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of reeling to all the surrounding peoples, and it will also be on Judah in the siege against Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of reeling to all the surrounding peoples, Arminian readers see Jerusalem becoming a cup that makes the nations stagger when they come against it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare the cup of staggering in Isaiah 51:17, 22 and the cup of wrath in Jeremiah 25:15. The siege also touches Judah, though the details are debated.

verses.text: It will happen in that day that I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all the peoples. All who burden themselves with it will be severely wounded, and all the nations of the earth will be gathered together against it.
verses.arminianNotes: It will happen in that day that I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all the peoples. Arminian readers see nations wounding themselves by trying to lift what they cannot carry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that all the nations of the earth will be gathered together against it. Readings range from historic to symbolic to future.

verses.text: In that day,” says the LORD, “I will strike every horse with terror and his rider with madness. I will open my eyes on the house of Judah, and will strike every horse of the peoples with blindness.
verses.arminianNotes: I will strike every horse with terror and his rider with madness. Arminian readers see the LORD throwing the attacking forces into confusion while watching over the house of Judah with care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase I will open my eyes on the house of Judah, a picture of protective care. The contrast with the blinded horses underlines the LORD’s defense.

verses.text: The chieftains of Judah will say in their heart, ‘The inhabitants of Jerusalem are my strength in the LORD of Armies their God.’
verses.arminianNotes: The chieftains of Judah will say in their heart, Arminian readers see Judah’s leaders recognizing that Jerusalem’s strength comes from the LORD of Armies their God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the leaders confess dependence on God rather than on their own power. Shared ground: both traditions see true strength as found in the LORD.

verses.text: In that day I will make the chieftains of Judah like a pan of fire among wood, and like a flaming torch among sheaves. They will devour all the surrounding peoples on the right hand and on the left; and Jerusalem will yet again dwell in their own place, even in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: In that day I will make the chieftains of Judah like a pan of fire among wood, Arminian readers see the LORD empowering Judah’s leaders to overcome surrounding foes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jerusalem will yet again dwell in their own place. The fire image pictures victory, and readers differ on whether it is historic, symbolic, or future.

verses.text: The LORD also will save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of David’s house and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem not be magnified above Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD also will save the tents of Judah first, Arminian readers see the LORD saving the countryside first so that the glory of David’s house and of Jerusalem does not overshadow Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the concern for humility and fairness among God’s people. No group among God’s people is to boast over another in the LORD’s deliverance of them all.

verses.text: In that day the LORD will defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He who is feeble among them at that day will be like David, and David’s house will be like God, like the LORD’s angel before them.
verses.arminianNotes: In that day the LORD will defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Arminian readers see the weakest among them made strong like David, a reversal of weakness through the LORD’s defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the remarkable phrase David’s house will be like God, like the LORD’s angel before them. Many Christian readers in both traditions see messianic hope here, held with care.

verses.text: It will happen in that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. Arminian readers see the LORD defending his people against all who attack them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse closes the first part of the oracle. Whether the nations are past, symbolic, or future is read in different ways across both traditions.
